title: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
description_short: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
description_medium: On May 16, 2020, Eric Trump told Fox News that COVID-19 would “magically” disappear after the election and claimed stay-at-home orders were meant to deprive his father of campaign rallies. He also said White House reporters wore masks only when cameras were on. The comments recast public-health measures as partisan tactics, without evidence for those claims.
description_long:
During a May 16, 2020, Fox News appearance with host Jeanine Pirro, Eric Trump called the coronavirus response a “hoax” and argued that state stay-at-home orders were intended to prevent his father from holding campaign rallies. He predicted the virus would “magically” disappear after the November election and claimed White House reporters wore masks only when cameras were present.

The comments came as the United States was responding to rising infections and deaths. Eric Trump framed restrictions as political efforts to hurt Donald Trump rather than as measures public officials said were meant to limit transmission. Pirro did not challenge the claims during the segment and added that Democrats wanted to frighten voters away from polling places. The interview turned public-health rules into an election argument, but it offered no evidence that state officials had issued restrictions to suppress rallies or that reporters used masks only for appearances. Those claims were made on television by Trump’s son during the campaign, not established as facts about the pandemic response.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump

title: Trump: Anthony Scaramucci warns that Trump is a threat to the nation, endorses Biden
description_short: Trump: Anthony Scaramucci warns that Trump is a threat to the nation, endorses Biden
description_medium: On August 24, 2020, former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci endorsed Joe Biden and warned that Trump endangered the country and the Constitution. He cited Trump’s treatment of democratic institutions, allies, the press, science and peaceful protesters. Scaramucci had served in the White House for less than two weeks in 2017.
description_long:
On August 24, 2020, Anthony Scaramucci publicly endorsed Joe Biden and urged Republicans to choose a different direction. Scaramucci had served as Trump’s White House communications director for less than two weeks in 2017. Before the Republican National Convention, he apologized for supporting Trump and described the president as a threat to the country and the Constitution.

In his statement, Scaramucci criticized Trump’s treatment of the criminal-justice system and democratic institutions, his attacks on allies and the press, his handling of science during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the use of force against peaceful protesters. He said Biden better represented the decency and institutional restraint he wanted the Republican Party to defend. These were Scaramucci’s stated reasons for breaking with Trump and backing Biden. The endorsement was a political judgment by a former administration official, not a formal investigation or finding about Trump’s conduct. Its significance lay in the public reversal by someone who had briefly held a senior White House communications job.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Anthony Scaramucci warns that Trump is a threat to the nation, endorses Biden

title: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
description_short: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
description_medium: Acting Homeland Security Secretary Chad Wolf told senators in September 2020 that Russia was actively interfering in the election and seeking to denigrate Joe Biden. He said the United States faced interference threats from Russia, China and Iran, but current intelligence did not show that China or Iran had carried out attacks. The testimony distinguished active Russian operations from broader threats.
description_long:
On September 23, 2020, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Chad Wolf told senators that Russia was actively interfering in the election and seeking to denigrate Democratic nominee Joe Biden. He also said the United States faced election-related threats from China and Iran, while intelligence at the time did not show that those countries had carried out attacks. His testimony distinguished Russian activity from the broader threat picture.

A separate Reuters report described a whistleblower complaint alleging that Wolf had told a former aide to stop preparing assessments of Russian interference and to reduce emphasis on white-supremacist activity. That allegation concerned how intelligence assessments were handled; it is separate from Wolf’s public testimony before Congress. The testimony recorded the threat assessment DHS presented in September 2020, while the complaint raised questions about the process behind it. Neither fact by itself proves that other countries had no interest in influencing the election or that every Russian operation had been publicly disclosed.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election

title: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
description_short: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
description_medium: White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows tested positive for COVID-19 around the November 3, 2020, election. Advisers said he began notifying people after early results came in, but the date he learned of his infection was unclear. Campaign aide Nick Trainer and other White House and campaign personnel also tested positive; Representative Matt Gaetz said he had tested positive for antibodies, not COVID-19.
description_long:
Mark Meadows, then White House chief of staff, tested positive for COVID-19 around Election Day in 2020. Advisers told the Associated Press that he began notifying people in his circle after early election results came in. The news became public later that week, but reporting did not establish when Meadows learned he was infected or whether he had symptoms at the time.

The reported cases included Trump campaign aide Nick Trainer and several White House and campaign personnel. Representative Matt Gaetz also told associates he had tested positive, but clarified that he had antibodies and did not have an active COVID-19 infection. The reports described a cluster of positive tests among people connected to the White House and campaign during a period of close political activity. They did not identify where anyone contracted the virus or establish a transmission chain. The key unresolved timing question was when Meadows learned of his infection and when he informed others, since the available account placed notification after early election results but did not give the date of his own test result.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19

title: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
description_medium: On November 5, 2020, Steve Bannon said on his “War Room” podcast that Anthony Fauci and FBI Director Christopher Wray should be fired and their heads displayed on pikes outside the White House. His spokesperson said he was referring metaphorically to Tudor-era executions. Twitter permanently suspended the podcast account, and YouTube removed the episode under its violence policies.
description_long:
On his “War Room: Pandemic” podcast on November 5, 2020, former Trump adviser Steve Bannon discussed what a second Trump term should do. He called for firing Anthony Fauci and FBI Director Christopher Wray, then invoked Tudor-era executions and said he wanted their heads displayed on pikes outside the White House as a warning to federal officials.

Bannon’s spokeswoman said he was speaking metaphorically and had not called for actual violence. Twitter permanently suspended the podcast account, citing its policy against glorifying violence, and YouTube removed the episode for violating its policy against inciting violence. The remarks were made while Bannon was free on bond in a separate federal case over alleged fraud involving a border-wall nonprofit. The episode documents violent political rhetoric and the platforms’ response; it did not describe a government order or an attack on Fauci or Wray. Bannon’s representative disputed a literal interpretation of the threat, and that response was part of the public record.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director

title: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers
description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers
description_medium: Facebook removed seven pages it linked to Steve Bannon, with more than 2.45 million followers combined, citing misinformation about voter fraud and the 2020 election. The Washington Post reported that the network promoted “Stop the Steal” claims. Facebook also restricted Bannon’s personal page from posting, but left the page online.
description_long:
In November 2020, Facebook removed seven pages it linked to Steve Bannon, which together had more than 2.45 million followers. The Washington Post reported that the pages promoted claims about voter fraud and the legitimacy of the election results, including messages associated with the “Stop the Steal” campaign. Facebook said the network used inauthentic behavior tactics.

The company also restricted Bannon’s personal account from posting, but did not remove the profile itself. Its actions therefore affected the network of pages and limited what Bannon could post on his own page while leaving that page visible. The report described Facebook’s stated rationale and the scale of the pages’ combined following; it did not establish how many people saw individual posts or believed the claims. The event was a platform enforcement decision during a contested election period, following online efforts to cast doubt on vote counting and the result.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers

title: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
description_short: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
description_medium: In a December 28, 2020, livestream, Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander said he planned the January 6 pressure campaign with Representatives Paul Gosar, Mo Brooks and Andy Biggs. He called the protest a “loud war” intended to put “maximum pressure” on Congress as it counted electoral votes. The lawmakers denied knowing him; the statement is Alexander’s account, not independent proof of an agreement.
description_long:
During a December 28, 2020, livestream, Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander said he had devised the January 6 plan with Representatives Paul Gosar, Mo Brooks and Andy Biggs. He said the four wanted to put “maximum pressure” on Congress while lawmakers counted electoral votes and described the planned demonstration as a “loud war.” Alexander said protesters outside the Capitol could influence Republican members.

The Washington Post reported that the lawmakers denied knowing Alexander, while he cited prior public events and statements as evidence of a connection. His livestream documents what he claimed before January 6, but it does not independently establish that each representative agreed to a joint plan or knew how events would unfold. The remarks described a planned protest and pressure campaign during the electoral count; they were not an explicit prediction of the later assault on the Capitol. The article therefore records a statement by an organizer about his claimed contacts and intentions, with the lawmakers’ denials also part of the account.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol

title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_medium: Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the NSA to install Michael Ellis as its general counsel in January 2021. Ellis began the job on January 19 and was placed on leave the following day, when the Defense Department inspector general opened an investigation into the appointment. He had been selected months earlier but not installed.
description_long:
On January 16, 2021, Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller directed the National Security Agency to install Michael Ellis as its general counsel. Ellis had been selected for the role in November but had not yet taken office. The NSA installed him on January 19, three days after Miller’s order and one day before the presidential transition.

On January 20, Ellis was placed on leave as the Defense Department inspector general opened an investigation into his appointment. Ellis had previously worked for Representative Devin Nunes and held intelligence roles at the National Security Council. The sequence raised questions about the appointment process because the position was filled immediately before the transition and the new general counsel was put on leave the next day. The linked reporting records the order, installation and investigation but does not establish that Ellis’s earlier work caused the inquiry or that the appointment was unlawful. At the time of the report, the inspector general’s review was ongoing.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer

title: Trump: Don Jr. gives deposition surrounding the misuse of funds by Trump's inaugural committee
description_short: Trump: Don Jr. gives deposition surrounding the misuse of funds by Trump's inaugural committee
description_medium: Donald Trump Jr. was deposed on February 11, 2021, in the District of Columbia’s lawsuit over inaugural committee spending. The questioning covered a nearly $50,000 hotel-room block contracted by the Trump Organization and paid by the committee. D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine said witnesses gave conflicting accounts and sought more time for discovery.
description_long:
District of Columbia Attorney General Karl Racine deposed Donald Trump Jr. on February 11, 2021, in a civil lawsuit over the 2017 presidential inaugural committee’s spending. The questioning focused on nearly $50,000 paid for rooms at the Loews Madison Hotel under a contract signed by the Trump Organization. Trump Jr.’s executive assistant handled the contract, which was signed by his friend Gentry Beach.

The District’s lawsuit alleged that the committee misused donations to benefit Trump family businesses, including spending more than $1 million at the Trump International Hotel. Racine told the court that witnesses gave conflicting explanations for the hotel-room charges and said Trump Jr. could not say whether the people associated with the rooms had donated to the committee. The deposition was evidence gathering in an ongoing civil case, not a ruling that the allegations were true. Racine sought additional time to collect records and question more witnesses, leaving the dispute unresolved at the time of the report.
organization_tags: Office of the D.C. Attorney General

title: Trump: The FBI publishes ‘Wanted' posters for Russians involved in 2016 election and more
description_short: Trump: The FBI publishes ‘Wanted' posters for Russians involved in 2016 election and more
description_medium: On February 25, 2021, the FBI began sharing wanted posters for Russian nationals tied to its investigation of interference in the 2016 election. The posters included Konstantin Kilimnik, wanted on obstruction charges, and people accused of conspiring to interfere with U.S. political institutions. The charges and allegations were not findings of guilt.
description_long:
The FBI began sharing wanted posters on February 25, 2021, for Russian nationals connected to its investigation of interference in the 2016 U.S. election. One poster named Konstantin Viktorovich Kilimnik and said he was wanted on charges of obstruction of justice and conspiracy to obstruct justice related to conduct in Washington from February to April 2018. The FBI said Kilimnik had ties to Russian intelligence; he had also received polling data from the Trump campaign in 2016.

Other posters sought people accused of conspiring to defraud the United States by interfering with the lawful work of federal agencies and reaching Americans through online operations. The group included Yevgeny Prigozhin, whom the FBI identified as a primary funder of Russia’s Internet Research Agency. The poster said arrest warrants had been issued in 2018. These were wanted notices and allegations in criminal charges, not convictions. The records describe the FBI’s search for the named individuals and the conduct alleged in the indictments; they do not establish that every person named was arrested or tried.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: The FBI publishes ‘Wanted' posters for Russians involved in 2016 election and more
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: The FBI publishes ‘Wanted' posters for Russians involved in 2016 election and more
